\section{Finite causal structures}

\begin{definition}[Finite causal structure]
A finite causal structure $S$ consists of a finite nonempty cut set $C_S$ and a function $L_S:C_S\to\mathbb{R}$ satisfying $L_S(c)\geq 0$ for every $c\in C_S$. The value $L_S(c)$ is the causal information destroyed by cut $c$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Integrated information]
The integrated information of $S$ is
\[
\Phi(S)=\min_{c\in C_S}L_S(c).
\]
\end{definition}

Finiteness and nonemptiness make the minimum meaningful without compactness or continuity assumptions.

\begin{theorem}[Minimum-cut attainment]
For every finite causal structure $S$, there is $c_*\in C_S$ such that
\[
L_S(c_*)=\Phi(S).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The image $L_S(C_S)$ is a finite nonempty subset of the linearly ordered set $\mathbb{R}$, so it has a least member. That member is the loss of some cut and is the defining minimum.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Comparison with each cut]
For every $c\in C_S$, one has $\Phi(S)\leq L_S(c)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The minimum of a set is no greater than any member of that set.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Greatest-lower-bound property]
If $a\in\mathbb{R}$ satisfies $a\leq L_S(c)$ for every $c\in C_S$, then $a\leq\Phi(S)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
The number $a$ is a lower bound for every loss and hence for the least loss.
\end{proof}

The preceding lemmas uniquely characterize $\Phi(S)$ as the greatest common lower bound of all cut losses. They also provide a recurring proof pattern: exhibit a feasible cut for an upper bound, and prove a common lower bound for all cuts.

\begin{corollary}[Nonnegativity]
Every finite causal structure satisfies $\Phi(S)\geq 0$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Zero is a common lower bound by nonnegativity of the loss function.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Zero-integration criterion]
For every finite causal structure $S$,
\[
\Phi(S)=0
\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
\text{there exists }c\in C_S\text{ with }L_S(c)=0.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
If $\Phi(S)=0$, a minimizing cut attains that value. Conversely, a zero-loss cut gives $\Phi(S)\leq 0$, while nonnegativity gives the reverse inequality.
\end{proof}

Thus exact reducibility has a precise meaning: at least one admissible intervention preserves all causal information represented by the chosen loss.

\section{Independent parallel composition}

\begin{definition}[Independent parallel composite]
For finite causal structures $S$ and $T$, define $S\otimes T$ by
\[
C_{S\otimes T}=C_S\times C_T,
\qquad
L_{S\otimes T}(s,t)=L_S(s)+L_T(t).
\]
\end{definition}

The product cut set is finite and nonempty, and the sum of nonnegative losses is nonnegative. This construction assumes independent cut selection and additive damage.

\begin{theorem}[Parallel composition law]
For finite causal structures $S$ and $T$,
\[
\Phi(S\otimes T)=\Phi(S)+\Phi(T).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Choose minimizing cuts $s_*$ and $t_*$. Their pair has loss
\[
L_{S\otimes T}(s_*,t_*)=\Phi(S)+\Phi(T),
\]
so the composite minimum is at most this sum. Conversely, every pair $(s,t)$ satisfies
\[
L_S(s)+L_T(t)\geq\Phi(S)+\Phi(T).
\]
Hence the sum is a common lower bound for all composite losses, giving the reverse inequality.
\end{proof}

\begin{example}
If the losses of $S$ are $2,5,3.5$ and those of $T$ are $1,4$, then their integrated-information values are $2$ and $1$. The six paired losses are $3,6,6,9,4.5,7.5$, whose minimum is $3=2+1$.
\end{example}

Repeated application gives $\Phi(S_1\otimes\cdots\otimes S_k)=\sum_{j=1}^k\Phi(S_j)$ for composites built by the same independent product-and-sum rule. Interacting systems need not satisfy this rule; their deviations from additivity may encode synergy or redundancy.

\section{Causal refinement}

\begin{definition}[Causal refinement]
A refinement from $S$ to $T$ is a function $f:C_T\to C_S$ such that
\[
L_S(f(c))\leq L_T(c)
\]
for every $c\in C_T$.
\end{definition}

A target cut is translated back to a source cut whose loss is no larger. This compares whole loss landscapes rather than merely comparing final scalar values.

\begin{proposition}[Identity]
Every structure has an identity refinement, given by the identity map on its cuts.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
The required loss inequality is reflexivity: $L_S(c)\leq L_S(c)$.
\end{proof}

\begin{proposition}[Composition]
If $g:R\to S$ and $f:S\to T$ are refinements, then the composite cut map $g\circ f:C_T\to C_R$ is a refinement from $R$ to $T$.
\end{proposition}

\begin{proof}
For every $c\in C_T$,
\[
L_R(g(f(c)))\leq L_S(f(c))\leq L_T(c).
\]
Transitivity proves the claim.
\end{proof}

These operations give a category-like calculus of causal descriptions.

\begin{theorem}[Refinement monotonicity]
If there is a causal refinement $f:S\to T$, then
\[
\Phi(S)\leq\Phi(T).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
Let $c_*$ minimize loss in $T$. The translated cut $f(c_*)$ belongs to $S$, and therefore
\[
\Phi(S)\leq L_S(f(c_*))\leq L_T(c_*)=\Phi(T).
\]
\end{proof}

\begin{corollary}[Composable monotonicity]
If $R\to S$ and $S\to T$ are causal refinements, then $\Phi(R)\leq\Phi(T)$.
\end{corollary}

\begin{proof}
Apply refinement monotonicity twice and use transitivity, or apply it once to the composite refinement.
\end{proof}

Thus $\Phi$ is an order-valued invariant. Refinements in both directions force equality of the corresponding integrated-information values, which motivates a future theory of causal equivalence.

\section{Exclusion among candidate complexes}

\begin{definition}[Candidate family]
A finite candidate family is a collection $\mathcal F=\{S_i:i\in I\}$ indexed by a finite nonempty set $I$.
\end{definition}

\begin{definition}[Exclusion value]
The exclusion value is
\[
\widehat\Phi(\mathcal F)=\max_{i\in I}\Phi(S_i)
=\max_{i\in I}\min_{c\in C_{S_i}}L_{S_i}(c).
\]
\end{definition}

The outer maximum ranks candidates only after each has faced its own weakest cut.

\begin{theorem}[Exclusion]
Every finite nonempty candidate family has a maximizing candidate: some $i_*\in I$ satisfies
\[
\Phi(S_{i_*})=\widehat\Phi(\mathcal F).
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The finite nonempty set $\{\Phi(S_i):i\in I\}$ has a greatest member, attained by at least one index.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Candidate upper bound]
For every $i\in I$, $\Phi(S_i)\leq\widehat\Phi(\mathcal F)$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
A maximum is at least every member of the set being maximized.
\end{proof}

\begin{lemma}[Least-upper-bound property]
If $\Phi(S_i)\leq a$ for every $i\in I$, then $\widehat\Phi(\mathcal F)\leq a$.
\end{lemma}

\begin{proof}
Every candidate value, including a maximizing one, is bounded above by $a$.
\end{proof}

\begin{theorem}[Unique exclusion under strict dominance]
Suppose $w\in I$ and
\[
\Phi(S_i)<\Phi(S_w)\qquad\text{for every }i\neq w.
\]
Then every candidate attaining $\widehat\Phi(\mathcal F)$ is $w$.
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The value $\Phi(S_w)$ is an upper bound for all candidates, while it is itself a candidate value. The two preceding lemmas imply $\widehat\Phi(\mathcal F)=\Phi(S_w)$. If $i\neq w$ also attained the maximum, strict dominance would give
\[
\widehat\Phi(\mathcal F)=\Phi(S_i)<\Phi(S_w)=\widehat\Phi(\mathcal F),
\]
a contradiction.
\end{proof}

Existence therefore needs only finiteness and nonemptiness. Uniqueness requires a strict summit; ties are not resolved by the basic exclusion rule.

\section{Finite combinatorics and algorithms}

For an $n$-element mechanism with underlying set $V$, represent one side of a cut by a subset $A\subseteq V$. A represented cut is nontrivial when $A$ is neither empty nor all of $V$.

\begin{theorem}[Nontrivial cut-count bound]
If $N_{\mathrm{nt}}(n)$ is the number of represented nonempty proper subsets, then
\[
N_{\mathrm{nt}}(n)\leq 2^n.
\]
\end{theorem}

\begin{proof}
The represented nontrivial cuts form a filtered subcollection of the power set $\mathcal P(V)$. Filtering cannot increase cardinality, and $|\mathcal P(V)|=2^n$.
\end{proof}

For $n\geq1$, this representation has the sharper count $2^n-2$. If complementary subsets represent the same unordered bipartition, quotienting reduces the count further. The theorem nevertheless establishes an exponential worst-case horizon.

\subsection*{Exhaustive evaluation}
Given a nonempty cut list and a loss oracle, initialize the current minimum with the first loss. Scan the remaining cuts, replacing the stored cut and value whenever a smaller loss appears. After processing $k$ cuts, the loop invariant states that the stored value is the minimum of the first $k$ losses. At termination it is $\Phi(S)$ and the stored cut attains it. For $m$ cuts and loss-evaluation cost $T_L$, time is $O(mT_L)$ and additional storage is $O(1)$.

\subsection*{Theorem-guided composition}
Naively enumerating a product requires $|C_S||C_T|$ pairwise sums. The composition theorem reduces this to two independent scans and one addition, costing $O(|C_S|+|C_T|)$ loss inspections. Pairing the two component minimizers also returns a minimizing composite cut.

\subsection*{Exclusion search}
For candidates $S_1,\dots,S_k$, compute each inner minimum and then scan the resulting values for their maximum. If candidate $i$ has $m_i$ cuts, the total loss-inspection count is $\sum_i m_i$, followed by $O(k)$ comparisons. Keeping all maximizing indices preserves ties; a unique winner should be reported only under strict dominance.

\section{Applications, scope, and limitations}

In causal network analysis, cuts may be graph bipartitions and loss may quantify severed influence. The zero criterion detects a partition with no measured cross-cut dependence, while the exponential bound explains the difficulty of exact scaling. In modular distributed systems, the composition theorem is both a computational shortcut and a testable consequence of the independence convention. In multiscale analysis, exclusion is a robust max--min rule: each candidate is scored by its weakest seam, and the strongest such score wins.

The refinement calculus contributes information beyond scalar comparison. A refinement provides an explicit translation for every target cut, so monotonicity follows from structural evidence. Two unrelated systems can share a scalar value without admitting any such translation.

The model remains intentionally abstract. It does not select a divergence, define causal repertoires, infer interventions from observations, or establish that high $\Phi$ is necessary or sufficient for subjective experience. It states consequences of a finite nonnegative loss landscape. Additivity is conditional on product cuts and summed losses. Exclusion need not be unique in symmetric or tied families. The exponential bound is a worst-case estimate, not a claim that every algorithm must inspect every subset.

\section{Future research}

Four directions are immediate.

\begin{enumerate}[leftmargin=*]
\item \textbf{Causal semantics.} Replace abstract losses by finite transition kernels, interventions, cause--effect repertoires, and divergence-based loss. Establish that these constructions instantiate nonnegative cut landscapes, and derive perturbation bounds for $\Phi$ and exclusion winners.
\item \textbf{Composition and exclusion.} Treat interacting composites and characterize conditions for additivity, subadditivity, or superadditivity. Develop exclusion modulo causal equivalence, including ties, and study its behavior under refinement and composition.
\item \textbf{Category theory.} Organize causal structures and refinements as a category, with independent composition as a monoidal operation and $\Phi$ as an additive order-valued invariant. Define equivalences and prove invariance under them.
\item \textbf{Combinatorics and complexity.} Quotient cuts by complementation, establish exact bipartition counts, and prove correctness and runtime bounds for branch-and-bound and symmetry reduction. For weighted graph losses, transfer approximation guarantees from standard cut problems.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Conclusion}

A finite nonnegative cut-loss landscape supports a compact calculus of integration. The minimum is attained, is nonnegative, and vanishes exactly at a lossless cut. Independent parallel composition makes it additive. Cut-translating refinements make it monotone. Finite candidate families possess exclusion winners, uniquely so under strict dominance. An $n$-element mechanism has at most $2^n$ represented nontrivial cuts.

These statements distinguish universal finite optimization facts from domain-specific assumptions about causal dynamics and consciousness. The central quantity has a precise meaning: $\Phi(S)$ is the cost of the weakest admissible seam. It is not a replacement for causal science, but a mathematical foundation on which richer causal models can be built.

For independent systems, a composite cut is a pair $(s,t)$ and its loss is $L_S(s)+L_T(t)$. The widget's partner slider demonstrates

$$\Phi(S\otimes T)=\Phi(S)+\Phi(T).$$

This is not a generic claim about interacting networks. It follows from the precise assumptions of product cuts and additive losses.

<details><summary>Click to reveal why the minima add</summary>
Pair minimizing cuts to show that the composite minimum is at most the sum of component minima. Every paired loss is at least that sum, which proves the reverse inequality.
</details>

{{demo:0}}

## 3. Compare causal descriptions through refinement

A refinement from $S$ to $T$ translates each cut $c$ of $T$ to a cut $f(c)$ of $S$ and requires $L_S(f(c))\le L_T(c)$. Identity translations are refinements, and refinement maps compose. Most importantly,

$$S\longrightarrow T\quad\Rightarrow\quad\Phi(S)\le\Phi(T).$$

<details><summary>Click to reveal the monotonicity proof</summary>
Take a minimizing cut $c_*$ of $T$. Then $\Phi(S)\le L_S(f(c_*))\le L_T(c_*)=\Phi(T)$. Along a chain $R\to S\to T$, transitivity gives $\Phi(R)\le\Phi(T)$.

## 4. Exclusion is a maximum of minima

For finitely many candidate complexes $S_i$, define

$$\widehat\Phi=\max_i\Phi(S_i)=\max_i\min_c L_i(c).$$

A winner always exists. If one candidate strictly exceeds every other candidate, it is uniquely selected. Equal values create genuine ties, as the widget shows.

The finite nonempty list of candidate values has a maximum, so at least one candidate attains it. If $w$ strictly exceeds all others, any different candidate has value below $\Phi(S_w)$ and therefore cannot attain the maximum.
</details>

An $n$-element mechanism has $2^n$ subsets. Nonempty proper subsets form only a filtered subcollection, so the represented nontrivial-cut count is at most $2^n$. This makes exhaustive evaluation exponential in the worst case. Complement symmetry, graph structure, and branch-and-bound methods are natural routes to improvement.

admissible causal cuts. -/

  (Finset.univ.image S.loss).min' (Finset.univ_nonempty.image S.loss)

theorem exists_minimum_information_cut (S : CausalStructure) :
    ∃ c : S.Cut, S.loss c = Phi S := by
  simpa [Phi] using Finset.mem_image.mp
    (Finset.min'_mem (Finset.univ.image S.loss) (Finset.univ_nonempty.image S.loss))

  exact Finset.min'_le _ _ (Finset.mem_image_of_mem _ (Finset.mem_univ c))

"""Numerical demonstrations for a finite calculus of integrated information.

A causal structure is represented by a nonempty mapping from cut names to
nonnegative losses. Integrated information is the least loss. The script
illustrates minimum-cut attainment, exact reducibility, independent parallel
composition, refinement monotonicity, exclusion, and exponential cut counts.
It uses only the Python standard library.
"""

from __future__ import annotations

from dataclasses import dataclass
from itertools import product
from math import isclose
from typing import Dict, Hashable, Mapping, Sequence, Tuple, TypeVar

Cut = TypeVar("Cut", bound=Hashable)


@dataclass(frozen=True)
class CausalStructure:
    """A named finite nonempty cut-loss landscape."""

    name: str
    losses: Mapping[str, float]

    def __post_init__(self) -> None:
        if not self.losses:
            raise ValueError("A causal structure must have at least one cut.")
        if any(value < 0 for value in self.losses.values()):
            raise ValueError("Every cut loss must be nonnegative.")


def integrated_information(structure: CausalStructure) -> Tuple[str, float]:
    """Return a minimizing cut and the integrated-information value Phi."""
    cut = min(structure.losses, key=structure.losses.__getitem__)
    return cut, structure.losses[cut]


def parallel_composite(
    left: CausalStructure, right: CausalStructure
) -> CausalStructure:
    """Build the product cut space with additive independent losses."""
    losses: Dict[str, float] = {
        f"({left_cut}, {right_cut})": left_loss + right_loss
        for (left_cut, left_loss), (right_cut, right_loss) in product(
            left.losses.items(), right.losses.items()
        )
    }
    return CausalStructure(f"{left.name} tensor {right.name}", losses)


def refinement_is_valid(
    source: CausalStructure,
    target: CausalStructure,
    target_to_source_cut: Mapping[str, str],
) -> bool:
    """Check L_source(f(c)) <= L_target(c) for every target cut c."""
    if set(target_to_source_cut) != set(target.losses):
        return False
    return all(
        source.losses[target_to_source_cut[cut]] <= target.losses[cut]
        for cut in target.losses
    )


def exclusion(
    candidates: Sequence[CausalStructure],
) -> Tuple[float, Tuple[CausalStructure, ...]]:
    """Return Big Phi and every maximizing candidate (preserving ties)."""
    if not candidates:
        raise ValueError("Exclusion requires at least one candidate.")
    scored = [(candidate, integrated_information(candidate)[1]) for candidate in candidates]
    big_phi = max(score for _, score in scored)
    winners = tuple(
        candidate for candidate, score in scored if isclose(score, big_phi)
    )
    return big_phi, winners


def represented_nontrivial_cut_count(n: int) -> int:
    """Count nonempty proper subsets: 2**n - 2 for n >= 1."""
    if n < 1:
        return 0
    return 2**n - 2


def demonstrate() -> None:
    """Run deterministic examples and assert every displayed identity."""
    sensory = CausalStructure(
        "Sensory loop", {"left/right": 2.0, "front/back": 5.0, "odd/even": 3.5}
    )
    memory = CausalStructure(
        "Memory loop", {"upper/lower": 1.0, "inner/outer": 4.0}
    )
    reducible = CausalStructure(
        "Separable relay", {"module boundary": 0.0, "cross boundary": 2.5}
    )

    print("MINIMUM-CUT PRINCIPLE")
    for system in (sensory, memory, reducible):
        cut, phi = integrated_information(system)
        print(f"  {system.name}: minimizing cut = {cut!r}, Phi = {phi:.2f}")
        assert phi >= 0
        assert all(phi <= loss for loss in system.losses.values())
    assert integrated_information(reducible)[1] == 0.0
    assert any(loss == 0.0 for loss in reducible.losses.values())

    print("\nINDEPENDENT PARALLEL COMPOSITION")
    composite = parallel_composite(sensory, memory)
    composite_cut, composite_phi = integrated_information(composite)
    sensory_phi = integrated_information(sensory)[1]
    memory_phi = integrated_information(memory)[1]
    print(f"  minimizing product cut = {composite_cut}")
    print(f"  Phi(composite) = {composite_phi:.2f}")
    print(f"  Phi(sensory) + Phi(memory) = {sensory_phi + memory_phi:.2f}")
    assert isclose(composite_phi, sensory_phi + memory_phi)

    print("\nREFINEMENT MONOTONICITY")
    coarse = CausalStructure("Coarse model", {"a": 1.0, "b": 2.0})
    refined = CausalStructure("Refined model", {"alpha": 1.5, "beta": 3.0})
    cut_translation = {"alpha": "a", "beta": "b"}
    valid = refinement_is_valid(coarse, refined, cut_translation)
    coarse_phi = integrated_information(coarse)[1]
    refined_phi = integrated_information(refined)[1]
    print(f"  refinement valid: {valid}")
    print(f"  Phi(coarse) = {coarse_phi:.2f} <= Phi(refined) = {refined_phi:.2f}")
    assert valid and coarse_phi <= refined_phi

    print("\nEXCLUSION")
    candidates = [
        CausalStructure("Local pair", {"c1": 1.1, "c2": 1.7}),
        CausalStructure("Recurrent core", {"c1": 3.1, "c2": 2.8, "c3": 4.0}),
        CausalStructure("Wide assembly", {"c1": 2.2, "c2": 2.9}),
        CausalStructure("Peripheral ring", {"c1": 1.9, "c2": 2.0}),
    ]
    big_phi, winners = exclusion(candidates)
    print(f"  Big Phi = {big_phi:.2f}")
    print("  winner(s): " + ", ".join(candidate.name for candidate in winners))
    assert len(winners) == 1 and winners[0].name == "Recurrent core"

    print("\nCOMBINATORIAL GROWTH")
    for n in range(1, 11):
        count = represented_nontrivial_cut_count(n)
        bound = 2**n
        print(f"  n={n:2d}: represented nontrivial cuts={count:4d}, bound={bound:4d}")
        assert count <= bound


if __name__ == "__main__":

concept.concept_description:
# Future directions

## Completed baseline

The accompanying Lean development settles the operator-algebraic core used by
Huang's spectral method:

- the canonical recursive signing satisfies `Aₙ² = nI` in every dimension;
- every real eigenvalue with a nonzero eigenvector therefore satisfies
  `λ² = n`;
- an eigenvalue bound `|λ| ≤ s` implies the numerical inequality `n ≤ s²`;
- the stronger conjecture that every signing has scalar square is false, with
  the unsigned two-dimensional cube as a formally verified counterexample.

The following are genuine extensions beyond that completed baseline.

## Prioritized extensions

1. **Connect the spectral certificate to Boolean functions.** Define Boolean
   functions on `Cube n`, pointwise and maximum sensitivity, and multilinear
   real degree. Formalize the induced-subgraph reduction in Huang's argument so
   that the operator theorem yields the full degree–sensitivity inequality.

2. **Classify scalar-square signings.** Replace the disproved arbitrary-signing
   conjecture by the face condition that every two-dimensional face has
   negative sign product. Prove both directions of the expected equivalence
   with `A² = nI`, then classify such signings up to switching equivalence.

3. **Multiplicity and characteristic polynomial.** For positive dimension,
   prove that `√n` and `-√n` each have multiplicity `2^(n-1)`, and derive the
   characteristic polynomial `(X² - n)^(2^(n-1))`. A trace-zero argument
   combined with the scalar-square identity should determine the
   multiplicities.

4. **Restriction and interlacing.** Represent the recursive operator as a
   finite real symmetric matrix, define principal restrictions, and formalize
   eigenvalue interlacing. This is the main bridge from density of a vertex
   subset to a high-degree vertex in the induced subgraph.

5. **Test tighter degree–sensitivity proposals.** After the Boolean-function
   definitions are in place, exhaustively enumerate small dimensions and
   record extremal pairs `(degree, sensitivity)`. Use these certified finite
   cases to reject false constants or lower-order improvements before pursuing
   general bounds.

6. **Beyond the binary cube.** Study signed operators on products of larger
   alphabets and on other Cayley graphs. Determine which anticommutation or
   face-cancellation relations force exact scalar-square identities and which
   corresponding local-degree bounds survive.
